title: The Shape of Fair Time
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
Our family scheduling argument began with a square drawn in blue ink.

It was supposed to represent Tuesday.

Katara had divided the page into days, with each day divided into morning, afternoon, and evening. She had written clinic shifts in neat columns. Aang's council meetings occupied the top half of the week. Toph's bridge inspections ran along the bottom in a handwriting large enough to be considered structural reinforcement.

My own commitments were squeezed into the margins.

"That's not Tuesday," I said.

Katara examined the square.

"It is literally Tuesday."

"It looks like a punishment."

Toph leaned across the table.

"Give me the calendar. I'll earthbend us a new week."

"We cannot bend time," Aang said.

"Then we stop pretending Tuesday can hold four people and the whole city," I said.
Katara tapped the clinic column. "These are patients. They don't disappear because I have a date."
"Nor should they. But you can ask which shifts someone assumed you'd cover for free."
Toph jabbed her finger at the bridge inspection. "Mine happens in daylight. Bad bolts don't schedule around romance."
Aang reread a council request. "They want me to settle the crossing dispute."
"Who asked? The neighbors or the secretary?" I said.
He studied the signature. "The secretary."
"There's the Avatar-shaped hole everybody throws work into," Toph said.
Aang wrote a question instead of an acceptance. Katara agreed to ask another qualified healer whether they wanted a paid shift. I put my Starwake errands in their own column and reminded everyone that my preference for polyamory did not turn every hour of my life into shared property.
Toph tipped back her chair. "Fine. Now we just need someone to invent a second Tuesday."
Aang brightened. "I could—"
"No," Katara and I said together.
For once he listened before trying to make the world more convenient.

"Then why are you the Avatar?"

He gave her the patient look he used when he was trying very hard to remember that he loved her.

I had agreed to the meeting because the previous week had been a mess. I was supposed to help Iroh at the pantry on Wednesday, check the supply ledger at Brasswatch on Thursday, and spend Friday evening with Katara, just the two of us. Instead, the bridge inspection ran late, Danse needed an additional sample, and I forgot to tell Katara that I'd promised to review a different set of measurements.

By the time I arrived home Friday, there were two cold bowls on the table and no one in the kitchen.

Katara hadn't shouted.

That was worse.

Now she sat across from me with her hands folded, waiting.

"Tell me what bothered you," I said.

"I waited," she answered. "Then I stopped waiting because I had an early shift. I don't mind that you help people. I mind finding out you won't be home from a note you leave after I've already made plans."

I stared at the calendar.

"You're right."

Aang looked relieved.

Toph snorted.

"That was fast. Usually people spend an hour defending themselves first."

"I can still do that if you want entertainment."

"No thanks."

Katara looked at me, not smiling.

"I know our relationships are complicated. I know we agreed we weren't going to measure affection by equal hours. But when we make plans, I need to be able to trust them."

"I agree."

Aang cleared his throat.

"I think I've done something similar."

Toph turned toward him.

"Only the part where you promise you'll be home by sundown and then spend three hours negotiating with a council because you don't want anybody upset."

Aang winced.

"That's fair."

"You're all painfully reasonable today."

"Give us time," I said.

The difficulty wasn't that we had too many people to love. It was that we kept mistaking good intentions for a working system. Nobody wanted to appear selfish. So we waited until the disappointment hurt enough to become an argument.

Katara pushed the blue square toward me.

"Tell me where you actually need time this week."

"Monday evening with you, if you want it. Wednesday I need a quiet night by myself. Thursday I'm with Iroh for the pantry inventory. Saturday I promised Greg I'd help set up the pier."

Aang nodded.

"And when do we spend time together?"

I looked at him.

"Do you mean everyone, or you and me?"

He hesitated.

"I meant everyone. But maybe I want both."

"Then we should write both."

Toph tapped the edge of the table.

"And stop treating the whole group as one giant person."

"Thank you," Katara said.

Toph leaned back, pleased with herself.

I wrote separate lines for individual time and group time. It looked less tidy. It was more honest.

We found out quickly that fairness was not the same as giving everyone an identical share of every week. Katara needed reliable advance notice because of her clinic shifts. Aang wanted space for spontaneous visits without making them obligatory. Toph preferred a whole afternoon of work and teasing to an evening of ceremonious romance. I needed time alone and time for other people I cared about. None of those needs were defects.

Then Toph made a noise like she'd swallowed a nail.

"What?" I asked.

"You've left a space for me on Friday."

"Do you want it?"

"I haven't decided."

"Then it stays open. No obligation."

She turned her head toward me.

"You don't have to keep a chair for someone who hasn't said yes."

"I know. I want to offer."

For a moment she looked almost shy.

"Maybe," she said.

I nearly fell off my chair.

Aang smiled into his tea.

Katara caught him.

"Don't."

"I'm not doing anything."

"You're glowing."

"Airbender condition."

Toph threw a napkin at him.

The calendar looked tidy enough to be suspicious.

Before I could congratulate us, Toph tapped the corner of the page.

“That's not a calendar,” she said. “That's a trap with very tidy boxes.”

Katara frowned. “We've left free time.”

“Free for whom? My bridge review starts at dawn. If I spend Tuesday night with you, I get four hours of sleep and then somebody asks me why the west supports are crooked.”

Aang looked at the row he'd marked for himself. He had set aside three consecutive evenings for council negotiations. He hadn't included the time he'd need to prepare.

“I thought I could finish early,” he said.

Toph made a derisive noise. “I thought I could teach the entire city to earthbend by lunchtime. We're both disappointed.”

I moved my own commitments out of the margin and onto a separate sheet. One belonged to Greg in Beach City, another to Danse at Brasswatch, another to a quiet evening I wanted entirely alone. The fact that Jasper was the person who traveled between the doors did not make the whole set of obligations flexible.

“I'm ethically non-monogamous,” I told them, “and I prefer polyamory. You know that. But a calendar doesn't turn all the people I love into one giant relationship with interchangeable hours.”

Katara nodded. “And being together doesn't mean we stop needing time apart.”

Aang took the brush. “Then we should put *rest* on the page first.”

“And no assigning *my* rest,” Toph added.

She drummed her heel against the floorboards while I marked my writing time. I was surprised at how relieved I felt seeing an empty square stay empty. Nobody filled it with a favor.

When the final version was ready, we agreed to try it for a week. A schedule could be an invitation to keep promises; it was not permission to make them for someone else.

I counted the squares once more, then realized I'd put three people's needs on Wednesday evening and left Thursday almost empty. It had seemed fair when I was filling in boxes. It looked less fair when I imagined actual people trying to get through a door.

"Can we test one week before calling this finished?" I asked.

Toph leaned back. "The schedule has homework now?"

"It always did," Katara said.

Aang agreed to handle Appa's morning care on the days Katara had clinic appointments. Toph wanted the bridge review kept separate from household chores, because having a gift for stone didn't mean she was available to fix every broken shelf. I wrote down my writing time and asked everyone not to treat it as an empty square simply because I would be home.

"How do we tell when somebody's overwhelmed?" Aang asked.

"Ask them," Toph said. "Revolutionary concept."

Katara laughed. "And believe the answer."

We tried a mock change: a clinic message arriving during a planned family dinner. Katara would decide whether she needed to go. Aang would check whether transport was required without volunteering Appa before discussing the return. Toph would not be drafted to babysit anyone's emotional reaction, and I would be allowed to say I was disappointed without making the disappointment an argument.

The first attempt was awful. We all talked at once.

"Maybe," I said, "we should practice one person speaking at a time."

Toph grinned. "Not a chance."

But she waited for me to finish. Aang went next, then Katara. The conversation took longer, and everyone understood more of it.

I thought about how long it had taken us to name the relationship as polyamorous, about telling each partner plainly that I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred love that could be shared honestly. A calendar couldn't do the loving for us. It could stop ordinary mistakes from becoming proof that somebody was unwanted.

By supper, the plan was imperfect but usable. Katara leaned against my shoulder while Aang cleared the table. Toph stole the last dumpling and claimed it was part of the test.

"Of what?" I asked.

"Whether you can survive disappointment."

"Apparently I can."

She smiled in the particular way that warned me she was pleased, then kicked my chair gently under the table. It was nothing like a formal vow. It felt more like a family.

We finished the calendar in an hour, which was astonishing considering how often Toph tried to rename Wednesday. We made one rule I cared about particularly: changing a plan meant actually telling the people affected. No silent assumptions that a loving partner would understand without being asked.

Then we discovered the missing problem.

The house had only one quiet room.

Aang used it to meditate. Katara used it to prepare clinic records. Toph went there when too much noise made it hard to concentrate on what she felt through the floor. I went there to write.

All four of us had been politely avoiding it when someone else was inside.

"Which means," I said, "we need to talk about the room as seriously as the relationship."

Toph grinned.

"Finally. A structural problem."

We spent the afternoon moving furniture. Aang made a low screen from cloth and light wood. Katara rearranged the shelves so medicines stayed in the proper light. Toph checked that the chairs could be moved without blocking the door. I measured the table twice and still got one dimension wrong.

Toph corrected me.

"You're terrible at lying to a ruler."

"I didn't lie."

"Your ruler did."

By evening the room had two workable areas and a sign that could be turned to say PLEASE KNOCK. It did not solve every issue, but it meant needing privacy didn't require giving a speech.

Katara found me there after dinner.

She tapped on the frame.

"Can I come in?"

I turned the sign over.

"Please."

She entered carrying two cups of tea and a small plate of dumplings. She set them down, then stood beside the table.

"I was still angry this morning," she said.

"I know."

"I'm less angry now."

"Good."

"Not because we drew squares."

"That was my favorite part."

She laughed softly.

"Because you listened. And because you didn't promise you'll never disappoint me again."

"I probably will."

"Probably."

I stood. Her hands were warm when I took them.

"I'm sorry I left you waiting," I said. "I will call or send word before the plan changes next time. Not afterward."

She stepped closer.

"That's what I needed."

The kiss was quiet at first. She brushed her thumb against my cheek, and I felt the pull of affection and embarrassment together, the strange tenderness of being forgiven without being excused. When I leaned in again, she smiled against my mouth.

"Monday," she murmured.

"Monday."

"Don't make me put it on a banner."

"Toph would."

"She would spell it wrong on purpose."

We laughed and stayed together until the tea cooled.

The next morning, Aang added an extra square to the calendar.

It read NO SCHEDULING DURING BREAKFAST.

Toph changed it to NO MEETINGS BEFORE DUMPLINGS.

Nobody objected.

It was the first schedule we'd made that felt less like a test and more like a way to give our choices somewhere to live.
